posts.text:
Bill Gates offered his childhood friend Paul Allen $5 per share to buy him out of Microsoft. Allen refused and kept the stock that would eventually help make him worth an estimated $40B.

Months earlier, while Allen was undergoing cancer treatment, he had overheard Gates and Steve Ballmer discussing how to reduce his ownership in the company they had built together.

The 2 had known each other since school.

Allen was 15 when he met 13-year-old Gates. They spent their teenage years working with computers and eventually founded Microsoft in 1975.

But the ownership split had been a source of tension from the beginning.

Gates initially wanted 60% of the company.

Allen got 40%.

Later, Gates pushed for another adjustment.

64% for himself.

36% for Allen.

Allen agreed.

Microsoft kept growing. Its deal to supply software for IBM's personal computer put the business on a completely different trajectory.

Then, in 1982, Allen was diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma.

He began radiation treatment and gradually reduced his involvement in the company.

One evening in December, he walked past Gates' office.

Gates was talking with Steve Ballmer.

According to Allen, they were discussing his reduced productivity and how they could dilute his Microsoft equity by issuing stock options to themselves and others.

Allen stopped outside the door and listened.

Then he walked in.

He confronted both men and left.

That evening, Ballmer came to his house to apologize.

Days later, Gates sent a handwritten apology.

6 pages long.

But Allen had decided to leave.

In February 1983, he resigned from Microsoft.

Gates offered to buy his shares for $5 each.

Allen wanted at least $10.

Gates wouldn't pay it.

So Allen kept his stock.

When Microsoft went public in 1986, Allen still owned roughly 25% of the company.

As Microsoft grew into one of the world's largest businesses, his shares made him one of the richest people alive.

At one point, his fortune was estimated at $40B.

The 2 friends eventually repaired their relationship.

But Allen never forgot the conversation he overheard during his cancer treatment.

Gates had offered him $5 a share to leave.

Allen left.

His shares stayed.

posts.text:
Bye bye Beehiiv 👋

I vibe-coded my own newsletter platform:

📧 Campaign management w/ editor
🖥️ Web archives (https://t.co/pypYdNhdlZ)
🔗 API support
🫧 List cleanup, deliverability reports

It took a few prompts with Opus 5.5.

I left Beehiiv because they raised prices for the 3rd time in 2 years.
- My first yearly bill was $1,000.
- My future bill would have been $4,000.

Now I'm using AWS SES + MongoDB, and I will pay less than $300/year.

Newsletter platforms charge per subscriber, when in fact the real cost is the number of emails sent. Subscribers will naturally become inactive, so you end up paying more for something that hurts your deliverability (sending to dormant subscribers = spam trap).

So I've set a cleanup cron job for my newsletter alternative. It marks inactive subs as dormant, sends one last re-engaging email, and stops emailing them. Money saved. Deliverability increased.

I also gain a priceless feature: Freedom. I can change the UI, add features, connect all my apps - anything is possible with just a prompt.

I'm replacing Resend next. I love it, but it's very expensive ($400/mo)

SNL TURNED A WHITE HOUSE RENOVATION INTO A HOME-IMPROVEMENT SHOW.

And that format choice is what makes the premise interesting.

“White House Makeover” takes the familiar language of property-renovation television and applies it to Trump's plans for the White House ballroom.

Instead of treating the subject like a conventional political report, the sketch borrows a format audiences recognize immediately.

The makeover reveal.

The confident hosts.

The promise that a big renovation will solve everything.

But the White House isn't an ordinary house, and a presidential building project isn't just another television renovation.

That contrast gives the satire its starting point.

SNL takes a political story and changes the lens through which we see it.

Suddenly, a question about presidential priorities becomes a parody of television's obsession with dramatic transformations.
